world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Hemmila, Ritva & Pirkko Luoma 2009 grammatical description of Urim (named in Wikipedia 'Urim language'); Foley 2018 Sepik-Ramu chapter gives Urim phonology but no stress statement was reachable

new_statements.quote: [p. 109] It has been somewhat difficult to determine what stress is in Urim. Perceived stress seems to be inconsistent, varying with different repetitions of the lexical item. [...] [p. 111] Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root. It is manifested by ±louder, ±longer, ±less ballistic (than the preceding vowel(s)) and -centralized vowel features. It has to have at least two of these features. Thus, neither are phonemic. These rules work within the root. [...] If the first syllable of a three-syllable word is stressed, the third syllable usually gets a secondary stress.
new_statements.citation: Luoma, Pirkko. 1985. Tentative phonemic statement of Urim. In John M. Clifton (ed.), Five phonological studies (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 31), 101-122. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: Section 4.3.1 'Stress', pp. 109-112 (deciding rule p. 111; secondary stress p. 111-112); scan pages 8-11 of the PDF
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (16-page image PDF, no text layer; journal pp. 102-116) and rendered PDF pages 8-11 (= journal pp. 109-112) to PNG; read them as images, not only the archive.org scanned. Section 4.3.1 'Stress' starts at the foot of p. 109. The quoted sentences are on the page images exactly as given: p. 109 'It has been somewhat difficult to determine what stress is in Urim. Perceived stress seems to be inconsistent, varying with different repetitions of the lexical item.'; p. 111 'Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root. It is manifested by ±louder, ±longer, ±less ballistic (than the preceding vowel(s)) and -centralized vowel features. It has to have at least two of these features. T…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not phonemic. Within the root it falls on the first syllable whose vowel is a full (non-reduced) vowel. A 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) reduces the first of two successive vowels to [ə] when the sequence goes from an open vowel to a more closed one or when the two vowels are identical, so such words are stressed on the second syllable (e.g. /ten.tar/ [tənˈtar] 'miserable', /ku.lu/ [kəˈlu] 'bottom'); words whose vowels go from open to more closed are stressed on the first (e.g. /ka.rek/ [ˈkarek] 'hen', /a.tok/ [ˈatok] 'white ant'). Stress is cued by at least two of: louder, longer, less ballistic decay, non-central vowel. The later Hemmilä & Luoma grammar as reported by Wood (2012:7) restates the same distribution from the other end: stress is typically final, always final in verbs, and initial in disyllabic nouns only when the first vowel is more open than the second. The editor's footnote 3 (p. 111) offers exactly that alternative formulation. Reading 'weight-sensitive' is chosen because placement depends on vowel quality (full vs. reduced/central vowel), not on a fixed edge; a catalog user could equally file it as 'fixed-initial with schwa-skipping' or, per Wood/Hemmilä & Luoma, as 'predominantly final'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 111: 'If the first syllable of a three-syllable word is stressed, the third syllable usually gets a secondary stress' (/met-en/ [ˈmetˌen]). p. 112: in reduplicated words 'All parts are stressed; the first one gets the primary stress' (/naŋ-naŋ/ [ˈnaŋˌnaŋ] 'sing-sing').
new_statements.exceptions: Author admits perceived stress is inconsistent across repetitions and that the analyzer did not settle it; a residue of disyllables (longer vowel in 1st syllable, louder in 2nd) did not fit either group. Nearly all disyllabic irrealis verbs have [ə] in the first syllable (hence final stress). Rule does not apply across morpheme or word boundaries (compounds, reduplication). Editor's alternative analysis: stress on the second vowel when more closed than the first, otherwise the first. Wood 2012:7 (Kalpm dialect, citing Hemmilä & Luoma n.d.:10) says verbs are always finally stressed and nouns typically so.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word level: 'These rules work within the root'; the vowel-harmony rule 'does not apply over morpheme or word boundaries'. Data are isolated words in a frame (230 di- and trisyllables) with a suprasegmental analyzer (pitch, length, loudness). Intonation treated separately in 4.3.3.
new_statements.identity_note: Luoma 1985 is a description of Urim proper (glottocode urim1252); its dialect statement is on the missing p. 101, but Luoma and Hemmilä worked on the Yangkolen (main) dialect per Wood 2012:8, so the 1985 data are most likely Yangkolen (Urim 1/2). Wood 2012 describes the Kalpm/Kukwo dialect (Nuku district, Sandaun; ~95% cognate with Yangkolen per Luoma 1992) and reports final stress there, e.g. the language name [uˈrim]. Glottolog lists no separate dialect glottocodes. Glottolog ref 23917 is a corrupted record (Healey & Steinkraus Tifal vocabulary concatenated with Hemmilä 1987 Helsinki MA thesis 'Urimin tematiikkaa', a Finnish-language thesis on Urim thematics) and was not pursued.

sources.note: Section 4.3.1 Stress, pp. 109-112: stress hard to perceive and inconsistent across repetitions; 230 di-/trisyllables run through a suprasegmental analyzer; rule: stress on the first full-vowel syllable of the root (a reduced/central first-syllable vowel throws prominence onto the 2nd syllable); stress and the central vowel are both non-phonemic; 3rd syllable of trisyllables usually gets secondary stress; reduplicants all stressed, first primary. sources.citation: Wood, Joyce Kathleen. 2012. Valence-increasing strategies in Urim syntax. MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics, Dallas. 180 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.2 Phonology, thesis p. 7 (Kalpm/Kukwo dialect): 'Stress in Urim is typically on the final syllable. In verbs it is always on the final syllable. In some two-syllable nouns, if the first syllable vowel is more open than the vowel in the second syllable, stress is on the first syllable; otherwise, stress on the noun is also on the final syllable (Hemmilä & Luoma n.d.:10). The vowel in unstressed syllables is often reduced to [ə] or [ɨ].' Also p. 70: verbs have final stress, -en suffix takes the stress; p. 89 fn 4: itna 'be.on' stressed finally, initial vowel reduced; language name given…
